messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Lina, a 37-year-old Southeast Asian American woman, had been working for years as a refugee aid worker when she was thrown to the ground by police during a chaotic street operation near an intake site she was visiting for work. She remembers the crush of bodies, bicycles swerving as people tried to get out of the way, officers shouting commands, and the sudden conviction that she might be badly hurt before anyone realized she was not a threat. What stayed with her was not only the force of it but the helpless public humiliation of it. In the months after, she had come to believe that what happened was profoundly unjust and that nothing meaningful had been done about it. She compared herself harshly to an imagined steadier, more competent person who “would never have ended up there,” and this self-judgment mixed with a painful sense that she no longer recognized herself.

Those beliefs began to shape what stood out as dangerous in daily life. At work, when police officers appeared near the shelters or transit hubs where she met clients, Lina’s attention snapped toward them before she even meant it to. In crowded waiting rooms or on busy sidewalks, especially if cyclists threaded through the press of people, she felt her body tense as if the same scene were gathering again. What frightened her was not just the reminder of the event but what it seemed to prove: that the world could turn arbitrary and violent without warning, and that she was the sort of person to whom this could happen. The sight of police, bicycles cutting past, or dense crowds could pull the memory back with startling force—the terror she had felt then, the grief that followed, and an emotional flood so strong she often had to stop what she was doing.

Because those moments brought back so much, Lina began organizing her life around not setting them off. She changed routes to avoid heavily policed areas, delayed client visits if the sidewalks outside were congested, and kept away from neighborhood festivals or markets where bicycles and crowds were likely. When an image or bodily jolt of the assault broke through anyway, she tried hard to force it out of mind, telling herself not to think about it. She also stopped saying yes to things that might have made her feel light or hopeful—dinners with friends, small celebrations with her husband, even quiet weekend plans—because any lift in mood felt fragile and somehow wrong, as if happiness would only make the crash back into terror or grief worse. Some evenings she turned to gambling for distraction and a sharp burst of feeling that briefly drowned everything else out.

These strategies did not settle her for long. The more Lina pushed the memories away, the more abruptly they seemed to return: the officer’s presence over her, the panic in her chest, the unbearable sense of loss afterward. After gambling late into the night or spending an evening grimly numbing herself instead of resting, she slept poorly, lying awake keyed up and irritable the next day. That edge showed at home and at work. She snapped more quickly at minor frustrations, and there were moments when she acted in ways she privately knew were reckless, taking unnecessary risks in transit or staying in tense situations longer than felt safe, as if part of her had given up on caution mattering. Those states of agitation made the memories easier to trigger again; on little sleep and already on edge, one glimpse of police near her office or one cyclist brushing too close could send her right back into the same overwhelming recall.

The memories themselves deepened the meanings she drew from the event. Each return of that terror and grief seemed to confirm that the violation was still unresolved, still unfair, still lodged inside her life. When she had to cut a memory short because the emotion became too much, she took that as evidence that she was no longer the person she used to be. And each time she avoided a gathering, silenced a thought, or lost herself gambling, she later judged herself for it, comparing herself again to someone stronger and more intact. That shame sharpened her irritability and restless risk-taking, and it made the next trigger feel even more loaded, because now police, cyclists, and crowds were not only reminders of what happened but reminders of what she felt she had become since.

By the time Lina sought help, the pattern had narrowed her life considerably. Her work environment, once a source of purpose, had become a place of constant scanning, and her husband had begun to notice how often she withdrew from anything enjoyable. She came in after a week in which a crowded client intake area, a police presence outside the building, and a cyclist weaving through the entrance left her shaken enough that she had to stop mid-conversation and hide in an office. What she fears most is that this is permanent—that the terror will keep overtaking her, that she will remain angry, sleepless, and unlike herself. What she hopes, cautiously, is to be able to do her work and return home without feeling that the worst moment of her life is always about to happen again.
